articles.title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK crowns winner as BBC axes the series
articles.summary: The UK spin off of the global hit show is being shelved after eight series on the BBC.
articles.body:
Warning: This article includes spoilers for the finale of RuPaul's Drag Race UK.

After 10 weeks of toe-to-toe lip-syncs, fierce runways and shady remarks, the time has come for one queen to be named the UK's next Drag Race superstar.

For the final time on the BBC, 12 contestants were whittled down to just one after the broadcaster announced it was axing RuPaul's Drag Race UK due to budget cuts.

On Thursday night, RuPaul crowned Flesh as the series eight winner.

The London queen snatched the title from Mocha, Naya Thorn and Alik, who also made it to the final episode.

The 26-year-old was crowned by last year's winner, Bones, who is also her best friend and drag sister, with the duo performing together as Heavenly Bodies.

Speaking to BBC Newsbeat after celebrating overnight, the Soho queen says the win still feels "surreal" and she spent the whole evening "smiling, crying, and laughing".

She will be the last queen crowned on the BBC before the UK edition moves to Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

While some fans have welcomed the prospect of a new chapter for the series which might include bigger cash prizes, like in other spin-offs, others fear leaving the BBC will mean less representation for LGBTQ+ culture.

Flesh says the move to Wow could widen the range of performers and subcultures featured on the show, but worries the shift to subscription could reduce the audience for drag.

"This is where it feels slightly sadder that we're leaving the BBC because for all of the parameters that it created that limited what we could do, there was more exposure than drag has ever been given," she says.

She admits she is "concerned" about the "knock-on effect" this could have on the future of the UK drag industry, such as creating fewer opportunities for contestants.

"Without that exposure, there will be less demand and with less demand and less exposure, events won't be able to be created," she says.

Amid this concern, Flesh encourages people to connect with their local drag community and performers to consider ways they can evolve performances to bring in new audiences.

The decision to shelve the programme was announced shortly after the latest series began airing , with the BBC saying it was facing "very difficult choices" amid "significant financial pressures".

Flesh was awarded the £25,000 cash prize after impressing the judges in the final maxi challenge, which saw the last four queens perform a megamix of girl group anthems from past series.

Wrapping the show's stint on the BBC this way felt like a "really fun and tasteful way to reflect on the iconography of Drag Race UK", says Flesh, who hopes the past contestants feel "honoured".

But she reveals the final group of queens did think the "writing was on the wall" for show's future when they were asked to do the mix.

Flesh has stood out across the series as a fashion queen, bringing looks to the runway that RuPaul said would go down in the series' history.

Speaking to RuPaul and judge Michelle Visage during the final episode, Flesh said Drag Race "tells people it's not only OK to be them but it's a gift and a dream, and to be crowned the UK's next drag race superstar would be mine coming true".

She made it through the series without ever being in the bottom two and only had to lip-sync for the first time in the final when the top three queens battled it out for the win.

After Alik was eliminated, Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn performed a rendition of David Bowie's Modern Love.

It wasn't only the UK's next Drag Race superstar recognised by RuPaul during the finale episode - the Miss Congeniality title is typically awarded to the friendliest and kindest queen.

This year that title was awarded to Paris Baby, who created more than her fair share of drama across the series, in particular her spats with Staffordshire queen KY Kelly.

Miss Congeniality is decided by a secret cast vote and the queens were visibly shocked when RuPaul said Paris had won by a landslide.

At the start of the series, Paris said she had been blocked on social media by some of her competitors, including Flesh, but said they were now "besties".

"Hopefully the world can now see there's a lot more to Paris Baby," she said.

articles.title: Anglesey women's-only running club harassed and followed by men at night
articles.summary: Môn Girls Run founder Gwen Owen says women facing harassment out running should not be normalised.
articles.body:
"What can we do? What more can we do to stop this? To have the safe, empowering space that we need."

Gwen Owen is the founder of a women-only running group and has taken to Instagram to express her despair at "intimidating" harassment she and Môn Girls Run receive from men at night.

"We're all glowing, we're in hi-vis, we had our lights on - we wanted to own the night - and we still got harassed."

During a recent 5K in Bangor, Gwynedd, men yelled and whistled at them out of car windows.

And they've also been followed by men who run alongside them.

North Wales Police officers have joined the group and witnessed harassment. Registration plates were recorded.

Owen, 28, from Anglesey, founded Môn Girls Run when she felt anxious running alone during the winter.

"I was running by myself for about six months, but then it started getting dark and I thought it was a bit scary going out on my own," she said.

After seeing similar groups in Manchester and Liverpool, she started her own on Anglesey.

"About six or eight women came to the first run, and I thought, 'yes, brilliant, I've created a community'."

Owen said female runners should not have to join a group in order to feel safe, "but for many, that has become inevitable".

"That's why the group is so important," she said.

Owen said harassment has become so common it is at risk of being trivialised.

"This shouldn't be normalised," she said.

"Because that's what's happening right now. People say, 'just ignore it, everything will be fine'.

"When I go for long runs on my own it happens much more often than people realise. I've had the same car pass me about five times before.

"We just want to be left alone. Even if you know us, don't honk your horn or shout at us, just let us run."

"We're always looking around and checking behind us," Owen said.

"We just want to be left alone and enjoy running."

The run in Bangor was part of the campaign Ein Nos Ni - Our Night, in English - by Welsh Athletics.

It aims to encourage women to run together on the 25th of each month to raise awareness about women's safety.

Owen said: "The evening was intended to empower women to go out and do things safely, but even when we are in a large group, it [the harassment] still happens."

North Wales Police has launched a campaign - Operation Cadence - to address harassment of female runners, and want incidents to be reported.

PC Catrin Hughes, who established the initiative, said: "As a police officer and someone who runs often, I understand how important it is to feel safe while running.

"Operation Cadence aims to build relationships, run alongside the community, listen to concerns and promote simple safety measures."

She said the initiative would involve patrols, including plain-clothed officers running on popular routes.

articles.title: After strangers raised more than $787,000 for him on GoFundMe, the Red Baron worker asked them to stop donating to his campaign and help other people in need
articles.summary: A Michigan grocery-store worker who became an internet sensation after confronting Instagram pranksters has asked supporters to stop donating to his
articles.body: A Michigan grocery-store worker who became an internet sensation after confronting Instagram pranksters has asked supporters to stop donating to his GoFundMe campaign after it raised more than $787,000. Walter Zerod, a father of four who works as a direct-store-delivery employee for Red Baron frozen pizzas, attracted widespread sympathy after a video showed him being targeted by pranksters pretending to take $10 from him through Apple Pay. The encounter prompted military veteran Luke Oakenshield, who had never met Zerod, to launch an online fundraiser to support him and his family. Thousands of people contributed, but Zerod has now decided to step away from the attention, citing concerns about his family's safety and privacy.Instagram prank on Red Baron worker sparks online supportThe incident reportedly took place in August 2026 at a grocery store where Zerod was stocking frozen pizzas. Two Instagram pranksters approached him and played a sound mimicking an Apple Pay transaction, claiming they had taken $10 from him. No actual money was transferred.The pranksters continued provoking Zerod as he tried to get on with his work. Frustrated by the interaction, he explained that he was under financial pressure, had four children to support and was working long hours. He also said he had already worked beyond his scheduled shift and needed to wake up at 5 am to visit 10 more stores.The video later circulated widely on social media, with viewers criticising the pranksters for targeting someone who was simply trying to earn a living.Military veteran launches GoFundMe for Walter ZerodThe online response prompted Luke Oakenshield, a military veteran from Arizona, to start a GoFundMe campaign titled 'Support a Harassed Red Baron Worker' on October 27, 2026.Oakenshield said he wanted to help Zerod after watching the video and learning about the pressures he was facing. Although the two had not met before the fundraiser began, the campaign quickly attracted donations from people who wanted to support the worker and his family.The appeal gathered momentum within days, eventually receiving contributions from more than 22,000 donors. The amount raised crossed $787,000 towards the campaign's original $900,000 goal.Oakenshield later established contact with Zerod and his family, and the two developed a friendship during the fundraising effort.Red Baron publicly backs its employeeThe viral video also prompted a response from Red Baron and its parent company, Schwan's Company. A company spokesperson confirmed that the incident had taken place in August and said the organisation had contacted Zerod to check on his well-being.The spokesperson said Zerod was doing well and remained a valued member of the team. Red Baron also acknowledged the attention he had received in a post on X on October 29, joking that its employee-of-the-month nominations were closed because he already had a fan club, including the company itself. The public message was seen as a show of support for the employee after the video brought his experience to a much wider audience.Walter Zerod pauses donations to protect his familyOn November 5, Zerod shared an update on the GoFundMe campaign, thanking everyone who had contributed money, shared the appeal or sent messages of encouragement. However, he said he wanted to pause donations and step away from the public attention.Zerod explained that his family's safety and privacy had to come first. He also said he was grateful for the opportunity to spend more time at home with his family following the overwhelming support. He confirmed that he would not be accepting interview requests and wanted the November 5 update to be his final public statement about the incident.Worker asks supporters to help other people in needRather than continuing to direct donations towards his own campaign, Zerod encouraged supporters to consider helping other people facing difficult circumstances.In his message, he suggested that those who still wanted to contribute could support another fundraiser, a local charity or a church helping families in need during the holiday season.He also acknowledged his friendship with Oakenshield and said he looked forward to staying in touch with the veteran. articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo's Christmas song sounds familiar... on purpose
articles.summary: The pop star sought permission from cult 80s band The Waitresses before releasing her festive single.
articles.body:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo unwrapped her first-ever Christmas song on Thursday night, alongside a festive music video starring Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon.

The track, called Take Me Home (4 Christmas), finds the pop star asking her boyfriend to "show some serious commitment" by bringing her to his parents' house for the Christmas break.

As soon as it was released, fans noticed similarities to The Waitresses' 1981 festive hit Christmas Wrapping... And it turns out that was by design rather than mistake.

Chris Butler, who wrote The Waitresses' song, posted a message on Facebook , saying Rodrigo had contacted him to seek permission for the song; and praising her "phenomenal" writing.

"About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be 'Olivia Rodrigo'," he said. "Said she'd written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it."

Admitting he'd never heard of the pop star before, Butler said he assumed the email was a fake.

But after researching her career, he became a fan - not just of her music, but of the fact she'd hired an all-female band, and negotiated control of her master recordings.

In the end, he decided to reply to her email - and posted the text to his Facebook profile.

"If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering," he said.

"They're really sweet and flattering... even if you AREN'T you.

"If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you, I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them.

He continued: "I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you "got" my songwriting, and that you like our band."

Butler also accepted the invitation to hear Rodrigo's Christmas song, and told his followers: "Her song was/is great.

"It's going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas number one contest they have every year in the UK."

Although the song is indebted to the Waitresses' new wave and post-punk sound, Butler does not receive a writing credit on Take Me Home (4 Christmas) as it neither samples nor interpolates any of his music.

Posting on social media, Rodrigo said it was written last summer with her longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, and Amy Allen, who has previously contributed to songs by Harry Styles, Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McCrae.

Meanwhile, the Christmas jumper-tastic video follows the single's storyline, with SNL star Ben Marshall playing her feckless boyfriend, and Nixon starring as her prospective mother-in-law.

Rodrigo's track arrives in the same week as several other major contenders for this year's Christmas number one.

Singer-songwriter Sam Fender has covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want for this year's John Lewis Christmas advertising campaign; while CMAT has teamed up with Elton John for a countrified version of his festive classic Step Into Christmas.

Alanis Morissette is releasing an album called Good Weather for Immaculate Conception, while Sufjan Stevens is issuing a compilation of his festive output, titled Worst Christmas Ever.

Chic legend Nile Rodgers has also teamed up with X Factor star Rebecca Ferguson to cover The Christmas Song (Chestnuts Roasting on an Open Fire), although the duo have received a backlash for using AI to create the song's video.

And Kate Nash has written a track called Christmas Eve , which tells the story of the night her grandparents met in Dublin.

However, all the new Christmas songs have the unenviable task of going up against Wham's Last Christmas and Mariah Carey's All I Want For Christmas Is You, which typically dominate the festive charts.

The two songs entered the UK's Spotify top 10 on 1 November, two weeks earlier than last year.

Wham secured the Christmas number one slot in both 2023 and 2024 - and could receive a sales boost this year, as fans mark the 10th anniversary of George Michael's death.

Last year's festive chart-topper was Kylie Minogue's XMAS.

articles.title: China's helicopter arsenal grows, is India ready for the Himalayan challenge?
articles.summary: The next shift in the military balance along the India-China frontier may not come from fighter jets or missiles alone.
articles.body: The next shift in the military balance along the India-China frontier may not come from fighter jets or missiles alone.China is increasingly turning its attention to the skies over the Himalayas, expanding the People's Liberation Army's (PLA) helicopter fleet with new attack gunships, heavy-lift platforms and multi-role aircraft designed to move troops, weapons and supplies across some of the world's most difficult terrain.From the Z-10 attack helicopter to the versatile Z-20 family, Beijing is building a more diverse rotorcraft force that could give its troops greater mobility and operational flexibility along the border with India.The expansion is not limited to adding more helicopters to its existing inventory. China is also changing the composition of its helicopter force, moving from a fleet that has relied on foreign-sourced platforms towards a wider range of domestically developed aircraft designed for specialised military roles.Russian-built helicopters, including the Mi-17/171 transport family and Ka-28 and Ka-31 naval variants, continue to serve alongside China's expanding indigenous fleet.According to a report by The War Zone (TWZ), the PLA now operates an increasingly diverse helicopter fleet covering battlefield transportation, pilot training, dedicated attack missions, airborne early warning and anti-submarine warfare. The report noted that indigenous designs are increasingly supplementing foreign-origin helicopters that continue to serve important roles in troop transportation and naval operations.This transition has been particularly visible in the development of China's Z-series helicopters. The Z-10 and Z-19 provide dedicated attack and reconnaissance capabilities, while the Z-8 family offers heavy transport and specialised support variants. The Z-20 has emerged as a central platform in China's modernisation drive, with variants developed for ground forces, airborne assault and naval operations.China is also developing a larger attack helicopter, tentatively identified as the Z-21, which could add another dimension to its combat aviation capabilities.China's helicopter edge worries IndiaFor India, the growing helicopter capabilities of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) have particular significance along the Himalayan frontier, where difficult terrain, extreme weather and limited road connectivity make aerial mobility critical to military operations.Helicopters allow armed forces to transport troops, ammunition, fuel and other supplies to remote forward positions, evacuate injured personnel and provide fire support to ground troops. They can also operate from forward landing sites that are inaccessible to larger transport aircraft, making them an important component of high-altitude warfare.The importance of helicopter operations in the region has been demonstrated repeatedly by the Indian armed forces. During Operation Meghdoot in 1984, the Indian Army and Air Force used helicopters to airlift troops to strategic heights on the Siachen Glacier. The Indian Air Force had also been operating helicopters in the region since 1978, when a Chetak helicopter made its first landing on the glacier.India's helicopter fleet and plans to counter ChinaIndia is relying on a combination of attack, transport, heavy-lift and utility helicopters to strengthen its military capabilities along the northern borders. Its existing fleet includes Russian-origin Mi-17 helicopters, indigenous Dhruv and Rudra platforms, American Apache attack helicopters and Chinook heavy-lift helicopters.New additions, particularly the indigenously developed Prachand light combat helicopter, are expected to strengthen India's ability to conduct combat and logistical operations in mountainous terrain.India also operates the indigenously developed Rudra, the armed version of Hindustan Aeronautics Limited's (HAL) Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) Dhruv. It is designed for armed reconnaissance, close air support and other combat-support missions. The Dhruv family also performs troop transportation, reconnaissance and search-and-rescue operations.India operates 15 American CH-47F Chinook heavy-lift helicopters. The tandem-rotor aircraft can transport artillery, vehicles, engineering equipment and other heavy military supplies to remote locations. The IAF also relies on Russian-origin Mi-17 variants, including the Mi-17 V5, for troop transportation, logistics, casualty evacuation and air maintenance missions.

articles.title: Armed police search near Gloucester schools after boy hurt
articles.summary: Police say a boy was taken to hospital with minor injuries.
articles.body:
A police presence remains in place at two schools after an altercation left a boy injured.

Armed police were called to St Peter's High School in Gloucester earlier after a male was seen with a "long-bladed item" nearby, police said. The school and Willow Primary Academy were put into lockdown while officers searched for the group who had fled the scene, police said.

The force said one boy had been taken to hospital with minor injuries and there was "no ongoing threat at the school". Both schools have now released students.

St Peter's High School pupil Jimmy said the situation was "really scary" and he was still in shock.

After getting into the Tuffley school for the day, he said his friends came in and told him something had happened near his home.

He said the school's alarm then went off and the computer he was on displayed a message saying "This is a lockdown".

"The computers are not accessible at all and we've all had to turn the lights off, lock the doors, turn all the blinds down, and we've had to get on the ground," he said.

"At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he added.

Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for two to three hours.

"[When police cars arrived] I thought this is getting serious, I'm getting worried, I don't know what's going on," he said.

The 15-year-old said he was able to message his mother when the school let students use their phones after about an hour.

"When I was able to eventually get out, she was giving me a bunch of hugs," he said.

"What I am is shocked. I'm surprised that this happened," he added.

Jimmy said the school had previously run lockdown drills but a real event had never happened before.

Adam, whose daughter attends the same school , said he felt frightened even though he had texted her and knew she was OK.

"I don't think this should happen at school. Thank God she is safe," he said.

The school had messaged parents to say everything was under control, he added.

Another parent outside the school gates earlier, whose daughter is in Year 8 and nephew is in Year 7, said the family was "so worried".

"I'm slightly calmer now the police have told us they're safe but I want to take them home.

"I haven't heard from them because they aren't allowed phones in school," she added.

Addressing parents outside St Peter's High School, an officer said a police presence would remain at the site for the rest of the school day.

"That is not there for a safety reason, it is to provide reassurance to yourselves and answer any questions. It is not because there is any risk or threat to anyone," she said.

Lorraine Campbell, an independent councillor who represents the Tuffley area, said although police stressed there was no ongoing risk, the incident was still "very concerning" and there was "a great deal of uncertainty".

"There is always a big shock when we hear of something happening very literally on our doorsteps, it's of great concern. Hopefully it gets sorted out as soon as possible," Campbell said.

"Anything like this is extremely troubling and disturbing - we are all concerned but we do all stand together on these things," she added.

Police, who were called to Chalford Road at 08:50 GMT, said no other injuries had been reported.

articles.title: ICE arrests foreign student at US airport while she heads for vacation with boyfriend
articles.summary: A 23-year-old UC Berkeley student from Colombia was arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents at San Francisco International Airport
articles.body: A 23-year-old UC Berkeley student from Colombia was arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents at San Francisco International Airport while waiting to board a flight to Portland for a vacation with her boyfriend, the Associated Press reported.Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez is currently being held at ICE's California City Detention Center. Her arrest has prompted protests and support efforts from fellow students and university officials, while immigration lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her detention.Albornoz Hernandez arrived in the US in September 2022 and overstayed her visa, but subsequently applied for asylum, citing severe gender-based violence in Colombia. Her application is still pending, and she had a valid work permit, according to her attorney Niko De Bremaeker of Centro Legal de la Raza.She was travelling to Portland with her boyfriend on Friday when an ICE agent in plain clothes approached her in the airport's departure area and asked her name. The agent reportedly guessed her identity three times before she confirmed it. ICE agents then separated the couple and informed her that she was being detained because her visa had expired.Her boyfriend, identified only as Anthony, described the arrest as frightening, saying he felt helpless as agents separated them.DHS defends arrestThe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed that ICE agents had detained Albornoz Hernandez at the airport. It said she had entered the country legally on September 6, 2022, with permission to stay until March 6, 2023, but had failed to leave after her authorised period expired.The department said she would receive due process and remain in ICE custody while removal proceedings were underway. It also maintained that having a work permit or a pending asylum application did not grant her legal immigration status.Her lawyers, however, have challenged the detention in a federal court, arguing that ICE officers did not present a warrant or assess whether she posed a flight risk before taking her into custody.The petition seeks her release and asks the court to prevent further detention unless the government establishes that she poses a flight risk or a danger to the community.University seeks her releaseUC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons also expressed concern over the detention, describing Albornoz Hernandez as an outstanding student and asking authorities to allow her to resume her studies.The arrest could be the first detention of an active UC Berkeley student by ICE since the Trump administration began its mass deportation drive last year, according to the university and her attorney.Albornoz Hernandez, who previously attended San Jose City College, was studying business administration at Berkeley and conducting research on artificial intelligence.She is scheduled to appear before an immigration court on November 17. Her lawyers' federal challenge to the detention is a separate legal proceeding.My recommended headline: US: UC Berkeley student arrested by ICE at airport while heading for vacation with boyfriendEditorial note: The supplied original is from Berkeleyside, not the Associated Press. articles.title: In 1963, a New York family paid $3,800 for a Georgia O'Keeffe painting; it spent nearly 40 years hidden under fur coats before resurfacing with a $2 million to $3 million auction estimate
articles.summary: A Georgia O’Keeffe painting acquired by a New York family for $3,800 in 1963 has resurfaced after spending nearly 40 years hidden beneath fur coats in an
articles.body: A Georgia O’Keeffe painting acquired by a New York family for $3,800 in 1963 has resurfaced after spending nearly 40 years hidden beneath fur coats in an East Village apartment closet. The work, titled Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, is now being offered by Christie’s in its 20th Century Evening Sale with an estimate of $2 million to $3 million, according to the auction house and reporting by the New York Post.The discovery began in 2022, when Betsy, a 65-year-old woman from Rhode Island, was helping her elderly aunt prepare her Manhattan apartment for health aides. Her aunt casually mentioned that there was a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet, a remark that eventually led to the recovery of a painting that had never been publicly displayed.A graduation gift from Downtown GalleryChristie’s records show that the painting was acquired by the family of the present owners from Downtown Gallery in New York on April 15, 1963. The purchase price was $3,800, and the work was given to the eventual owner as a graduation present by her mother. The painting is an oil on canvas measuring 10 by 24 inches. It was painted in 1930, signed by O’Keeffe with her initials inside her distinctive star device, and titled and dated Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I on its original backing board.Before entering the family’s collection, the work had an early exhibition history. Christie’s lists it as having been shown at An American Place in New York in 1931, in an exhibition titled Georgia O’Keeffe: Recent Paintings.Why it disappeared into a closetThe painting hung in the aunt’s apartment until the 1980s, according to Betsy. At that point, her aunt became uncomfortable after a guest appeared overly interested in the work, and she decided to store it away rather than continue displaying it. The painting was placed in its original packaging and kept under a line of fur coats for nearly four decades. When Betsy finally retrieved it a few weeks before the auction announcement, the box still bore its original gallery label.Betsy said her aunt understood the painting’s value and saw it as a reflection of her financial standing, but preferred not to draw attention to herself. Her aunt, a former Foreign Service employee described by family as private and accomplished, passed away shortly after the painting was found at the age of 98.A rare O’Keeffe landscapeNear Abiquiu, New Mexico I captures the undulating hills of New Mexico in the softened, abstract style for which O’Keeffe became known. The work reflects the artist’s deep connection to the southwestern landscape, a subject that became central to her career.Christie’s describes the painting as a seminal work representing that connection. The auction house’s international director of American art said discoveries like this are rare in the established market for historically significant American artists.The painting’s existence had previously been confirmed only through a photograph taken in 1931. Its reappearance in its original packaging, with the gallery label intact, gives collectors and scholars a unusually direct link to its early history.What Christie’s expectsChristie’s has listed the work as lot 34A in its 20th Century Evening Sale, with an estimate of $2 million to $3 million. The New York Post reported that the estimate is in the region of $3 million, reflecting the painting’s rarity, condition and provenance.The painting's bidding starts on November 18, as per Christie's website. Before the sale, Christie’s planned to display it during a complimentary public exhibition from November 7 to 17 at 20 Rockefeller Center in New York, as per NY Post.The contrast with its 1963 purchase price is striking. A $3,800 acquisition has become a multimillion-dollar auction lot, a result shaped by O’Keeffe’s enduring market strength and the painting’s long absence from public view.What happens to the proceedsBetsy said a portion of the sale proceeds will be donated to an educational institution. The remainder will go to her and her relatives, with possible uses including paying off a mortgage.The family has requested privacy and has not publicly identified the late owner. Their decision to sell, however, means that a painting hidden from view for decades will now be seen by collectors and the public before it changes hands.For O’Keeffe’s market, the sale is another reminder of how significant works can remain unseen for generations. A painting bought for $3,800 in 1963, stored beneath fur coats for nearly 40 years, is now expected to bring between $2 million and $3 million at auction.You use AI every day. articles.title: Self-styled 'king of Germany' goes on trial accused of heading criminal group
articles.summary: Peter Fitzek is a member of a banned Reichsbürger group that sought to set up the "Kingdom of Germany" (KRD).
articles.body:
A self-declared "king" of Germany has gone on trial in Düsseldorf accused of leading a criminal organisation along with three other men described as his senior "subjects".

Peter Fitzek, who calls himself Peter the First, is a member of a banned Reichsbürger (Citizens of the Reich) group that sought to set up a "Kingdom of Germany" (KRD).

Reichsbürger are defined by German intelligence agencies as conspiracy theorists who reject the existence and legitimacy of the post-war German state.

The defendants are accused of plotting against Germany by seeking to establish the structures of an alternative state, including a banking and insurance system and currency.

His defence lawyers announced that he would be making a detailed statement.

The defendants, including Fitzek and three other men identified only as Benjamin M, Mathias B and Martin S, face up to 10 years in prison.

In 2012, Fitzek, a former chef and karate instructor, declared himself "supreme sovereign" of the "kingdom" and had himself crowned, dressed in ermine robes and brandishing a medieval sword.

Fitzek began buying land and property across the country. With around 6,000 members, the KRD became the largest Reichsbürger and self-governance group in Germany.

In 2025, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt banned the KRD, and Fitzek and the other three suspects were taken into custody.

Prosecutors accuse the group of founding the KRD "to replace the 'system' of the Federal Republic of Germany".

They allege that the organisation operated a banking and insurance system with branches in Dresden, Ulm, Menden and Lutherstadt Wittenberg, as well as a "registration office" that issued fake identity documents and its own currency.

Further charges include organised forgery and tax evasion amounting to millions of euros.

In just five years up to 2025, the KRD is alleged to have taken in about €10m (£8.25m) through unauthorised banking and insurance transactions, as well as via donations, gifts and fee-based seminars.

Prosecutors say these revenues were not declared to the tax authorities and that no income tax or social security contributions were paid on behalf of employees.

The KRD is also accused of recruiting other companies by promising them that they would be able to operate free of tax and duties.

In an interview with the BBC in 2022, Fitzek denied having any violent intentions, but labelled the German state as "destructive and sick".

Intelligence services believe some 26,000 people are part of Reichsbürger organisations in Germany.

The groups are very diverse, and intelligence services say a small minority are right-wing extremists and potentially violent.

In a separate case in 2022, dozens of people were arrested, many of them Reichsbürger, for plotting to overthrow the German government in Berlin.

They were accused of planning a violent coup, which included kidnapping the health minister, to create "civil war conditions" to bring down German democracy.

Five people were jailed last year over that plot.

articles.title: Russell Brand faces 'significant' prison sentence after rape and sexual assault conviction
articles.summary: A jury found the actor guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
articles.body:
Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison term after his rape and sexual assault conviction, a judge has said.

A jury in London found the British comedian and actor guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault Thursday. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. The judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on Monday, Nov. 9.

"You've been convicted of a number of offenses including rape," judge Joel Bennathan said. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."

The actor had been charged on seven counts: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Following Thursday's verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women.

"The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims.

The head of the Met Police, Sir Mark Rowley, has urged any other victims of Brand to contact the police.

"There's two more rape allegations that we're looking at. We're encouraging anybody else to come forward if there's any other allegations," he told British media on Friday.

He later said that he "wouldn't be surprised if many, many more come forward," adding of the trial, "This shows that powerful people can be brought down so you are safe stepping forward and we will support and try and bring that person to justice."

Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year.

He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012.

The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but all of them came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women.

During the trial, the court heard tearful and forceful testimony from the six complainants, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity.

The convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a victim who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his shows. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process.

Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004.

He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin.

A third complaint of sexual assault ended in a guilty verdict when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her.

Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

CCTV footage released by the Met Police after the verdict shows Brand being interviewed by police in custody in December 2023.

"As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity."

He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined."

Following the verdict, the judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody.

In a statement, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Met Police, said: "Today's verdict is first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

The statement added: "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women.

"As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

Ron Brand, Russell's father, told the BBC he was "shocked" by the verdicts. "I just didn't expect this — it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating."

articles.title: In January 2025, Milo Ventimiglia lost his family home and a second house under construction to the Los Angeles fires while his wife was 38 weeks pregnant; in November 2026, he said they had found a new home
articles.summary: Actor Milo Ventimiglia has shared an update on his family's life nearly two years after the Los Angeles wildfires destroyed their home and another house
articles.body: Actor Milo Ventimiglia has shared an update on his family's life nearly two years after the Los Angeles wildfires destroyed their home and another house they were preparing to move into. In January 2025, the This Is Us actor and his wife, Jarah Mariano, lost both properties in the fires. At the time, Mariano was 38 weeks pregnant with their first child.Speaking to Us Weekly in an interview published on November 2, Ventimiglia said the family had settled into a new home. The actor, now 49, said he, his wife and their two young children were doing well. He described their present home and surroundings as wonderful and said they were now close to family and friends."It's good. The kids have no idea what happened. Wife and I are good. We're settled. We're in a wonderful home, in a wonderful place, around some good family and friends," he said.However, the actor said the family was still dealing with the practical consequences of losing their properties. While they had moved past much of the emotional distress, some aspects of the experience remained unresolved. He described losing everything they owned while also trying to rebuild their lives as a complicated experience.On January 7, 2025, they evacuated as the Palisades Fire spread through the area. They lost the house they were living in, along with another property that was under construction and close to being ready for them to move into.Two weeks after the fires, the couple welcomed their first child, a daughter named Ke'ala Coral Ventimiglia. Mariano announced the birth on January 31, 2025, through an Instagram post. She also spoke about the family's losses and their plans to begin again. "Houseless, never homeless," she wrote while announcing their daughter's arrival.Mariano said that the family had lost their home and everything they owned, but she was grateful that they were together, safe and healthy. She also thanked the people who had supported them during the difficult period.Milo Ventimiglia says memories remainLooking back at the fires, Ventimiglia said the experience taught him about perseverance. He explained that losing material possessions did not mean losing the memories associated with them.He recalled an unusual habit that began immediately after the fires. Every one or two minutes, he would suddenly remember an object that had been part of his life. He began writing down those objects because each one brought back a particular memory.As time passed, these recollections became less frequent. What initially happened every few minutes gradually happened after longer intervals, sometimes days or weeks apart."But that object was always attached to a memory, and I would write down the object to retain or recall the memory. Object is gone. Memory is still there," he said.The actor said the experience had changed how he looked at the loss. While acknowledging that losing everything was difficult, he also spoke about finding gratitude in the life he and Mariano had built since then.He said that looking at his wife, children and new home made him consider how their lives might have taken a different direction if the fires had not happened."I'm like, 'Well, we probably wouldn't be in this direction had that not happened.' So you kind of have to be grateful for the big, ugly event," he said.However, he also acknowledged that the experience was complicated and that people affected by the fires would respond to it differently.The actor said he and his wife had moved beyond much of the emotional impact, but the business-related matters were still ongoing.Actor says raising two children has changed his lifeVentimiglia also spoke about life with his wife and their two young children. Asked about the best part of being a father, he said watching the children discover things for the first time was particularly special.He said their reactions to everyday things brought him happiness. Seeing them experience something new made even simple moments memorable."Honestly, when the kids smile, it's the most wonderful thing. articles.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
articles.summary: The behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution also helped elevate him, writes the BBC's media editor Katie Razzall.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court , following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.

He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.

Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.

With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.

He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.

Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.

Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.

The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.

"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."

But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.

"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.

"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."

He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".

The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".

Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".

But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".

In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?

A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."

Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".

"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"

And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".

"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.

At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

articles.title: Record sightings of rare moth in Glen Affric
articles.summary: The Affric Twitcher is found almost exclusively in the Highland glen.
articles.body:
A record number of sightings have been made of a moth that is found almost exclusively in Glen Affric in the Highlands.

The Affric Twitcher, also known by its scientific name Choreutis diana, is one of the UK's rarest species of moth.

A local recorder, Mike Taylor, saw 43 adult moths during a two-day visit to the glen - the highest number for the area since records began in 2021.

Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS), which manages woodland in Glen Affric, said the sightings highlighted the importance of protecting biodiversity.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Staff and volunteers from Butterfly Conservation also recorded 111 silk structures called larval spinnings in the area.

Patrick Cook, from the organisation, said: "The Affric Twitcher depends on native birch woodland, where its larvae feed on leaves and create distinctive canoe-shaped silken shelters known as spinnings"

Surveys were conducted in parts of Glen Affric, which has areas of surviving native Caledonian Forest , including around Loch Beinn a' Mheadhoin.

Evidence of the moth was found in new areas and its range is believed to have doubled in two years.

Shona Amos, an FLS environmental forester, said deer management, removal of non-native plants and regeneration of birch woodland had played a part in helping the moth and other wildlife.

articles.title: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
articles.summary: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.
articles.body:
The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe .

The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.

Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".

The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.

It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.

It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.

Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".

One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.

Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.

Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".

"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes .

One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.

The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.

As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".

Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.

"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.

"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.

articles.body: Anakh Sawhney was nine years old when she began helping children who did not have enough food to eat. Her effort has since grown into a nonprofit supporting more than 110,000 people across five US states and several regions in India.Anakh, now 17, founded Rice Kids in 2018 after meeting children at homeless shelters where her family volunteered. Their circumstances made her think about how she could help. She began by focusing on one immediate need: providing food to children who were going hungry.Over the years, however, her work expanded beyond meals. Rice Kids now focuses on addressing the reasons that keep children from accessing education and other basic support. Its programmes include nutrition, education, health support, school supplies, computers and clothing.The organisation has also built partnerships with hundreds of shelters, community centres and educational organisations. These partnerships help it reach families and children who need support in different communities.Anakh's work has also extended to India, where Rice Kids supports children from marginalised communities. More than half of the students supported by the organisation in India have returned to mainstream education. They no longer have to worry about how to put food on their families' tables, according to the Barron Prize profile.How Rice Kids expanded beyond food supportRice Kids was founded in 2018 with the aim of providing hot meals to hungry children. As the initiative developed, Anakh began looking at the wider problems affecting the families it wanted to support.Food insecurity was not the only difficulty these children faced. Limited access to education and other essential resources could also affect their opportunities.The organisation gradually expanded its work to address these needs. Along with nutrition, it began providing educational programmes, health support, school supplies, computers and clothing.Rice Kids now works with hundreds of shelters, community centres and educational organisations. These partnerships help the nonprofit deliver its programmes to children and families across different locations.Its work is spread across five US states and several regions in India. The organisation says it has supported more than 110,000 people through its initiatives.Helping children return to mainstream education in IndiaEducation is an important part of Rice Kids' work, particularly among children from marginalised communities in India.The organisation aims to remove some of the barriers that prevent children from attending school. Its support includes educational programmes and essential resources that families may otherwise struggle to access.According to the Barron Prize profile, more than half of the students supported by Rice Kids in India have returned to mainstream education.The organisation has also focused on making its work sustainable within the communities it serves. It trains women from marginalised communities to become educators. This approach allows local women to take part in delivering educational support.Anakh on what she learnt from working with familiesAnakh says listening to families has been an important part of understanding what kind of support they actually need. articles.title: Plans unveiled to modernise Abbey House Museum in Leeds
articles.summary: Proposals for Abbey House Museum in Kirkstall include an upgrade to its Victorian streets.
articles.body:
Plans have been unveiled to modernise a Grade II listed Leeds museum that was previously at risk of closure.

Abbey House Museum in Kirkstall was put forward for closure during the city council's budget proposals in 2024 - but was saved after a "passionate" response to a public consultation.

Plans for the museum, which opened in 1927, include upgrades to its replica Victorian streets to include hands-on immersive experiences, and new exhibition spaces.

Councillor Salma Arif, Leeds City Council's executive member for economy, said the proposals marked a "bold new direction" for the museum.

The plans come as part of a Reimagining Project supported by Leeds City Council and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport's Museum Renewal Fund.

They have been drawn up following consultations with staff, local history groups and families.

There are also hopes to explore the building's centuries-old roots, such as its original role as the gatehouse of Kirkstall Abbey until the dissolution of the monasteries.

An exhibition is planned for 2027 to celebrate the museum's centenary.

Thousands of people signed a petition against the museum's closure when it was initially suggested in 2024, with nearly 10,000 taking part in consultations with the council.

Arif said: "During the public consultation on the museum's future, what really came across was the passion and determination people have to see the site succeed.

"We want to channel that enthusiasm into creating an attraction which can continue to welcome visitors for many years to come."

A community information session to outline the plans will take place at the museum on Sunday.

The proposals will be discussed with the community, staff and key stakeholders before a development application for external funding is submitted.

articles.title: Michael Jordan's Brand Wings initiative has supported more than 4,000 scholarship recipients worldwide; its 10th anniversary programme awarded over 350 scholarships in 2025

articles.body: Michael Jordan's Jordan Brand has marked the 10th anniversary of its Wings initiative after helping more than 4,000 students worldwide access educational opportunities through scholarships, mentorship and creative programmes. The initiative, established to help young people overcome barriers to education and personal development, reached another milestone in 2025 by awarding scholarships to more than 350 students across the United States, the Philippines and China. The anniversary also brought new partnerships in London and Paris, alongside programmes designed to extend its support to more communities.Jordan Brand Wings has supported more than 4,000 scholarship recipientsThe Wings initiative is one of Jordan Brand's major community programmes, drawing inspiration from Michael Jordan's achievements and his personal connection to education. According to Nike's official announcement published on July 15, 2025, the programme has provided opportunities to more than 4,000 scholars worldwide over its first decade.The initiative was developed around the belief that access to education, guidance and encouragement can help young people reach their potential. It also reflects the importance of education in Jordan's own upbringing, with his parents instilling in him the value of learning.Jordan Brand's official Wings website explains that its purpose is to create inspiration and access that help young people build better futures. The programme also recognises that not every student has the same opportunities, particularly those from disadvantaged communities who face additional barriers to education and professional development.Instead of concentrating on financial assistance alone, Wings combines scholarships with mentorship, practical experience and opportunities to explore creative interests. Its activities are designed to help students develop skills that can support them beyond their education and into their future careers.The 2025 scholarship programme reached students across three countriesThe 10th anniversary celebrations in 2025 included scholarships for more than 350 students from several locations in the United States, the Philippines and China.Nike's announcement identified recipients from Charlotte, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, Philadelphia and Portland in the US, as well as Manila in the Philippines and 33 cities across China. These students joined an established international community of more than 4,000 people who had benefited from the initiative during its first decade.The scholarships are part of the Wings Scholars Program, which aims to make higher education more accessible. The programme works with local partners to identify committed students, primarily those who would be the first in their families to attend university.Its support includes scholarships, information and educational resources intended to reduce the difficulties students may encounter while completing their studies. The programme has a particular interest in helping students pursue opportunities in creative fields, teaching, coaching and sport.What other opportunities does the Wings initiative provideScholarships are only one part of the initiative. Jordan Brand has also developed programmes that introduce young people to creative industries, professional environments and experiences beyond the classroom.One of these is the Beyond Basketball programme, which uses sport as a starting point for wider learning. articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
articles.body:
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.

"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.

The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.

Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.

Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.

However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.

"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.

Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.

They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.

Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".

Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.

Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.

Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.

One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.

The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.

Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.

The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.

The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.

"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.

"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."

The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.

Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.

The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

articles.title: 16 Canadians moved to Florida in 2022 on instruction of cult leader Liana Shanti. After years of legal battle, 3 get $56 million in defamation case
articles.summary: Three Canadians from Saskatchewan have been awarded more than C$56 million in damages after a Hawaii jury found that an online spiritual teacher had
articles.body: Three Canadians from Saskatchewan have been awarded more than C$56 million in damages after a Hawaii jury found that an online spiritual teacher had defamed them through an alleged campaign of online harassment, accusing them of child abuse, supporting paedophiles and practising black magic.The jury ordered Liane Wilson, who operates online under the name Liana Shanti, to pay Paula Haygarth and Byron and Stefanie Horvath US$40.1 million (more than C$56 million). The award is among the largest civil damages verdicts in Hawaii's history.The verdict followed a four-year legal battle that began after Shanti sued the Canadians, accusing them of defaming her through online posts that described her as a fraudster and cult leader who broke up families. The three Canadians filed counterclaims, alleging that Shanti had targeted them with an online hate campaign.An eight-member jury in Honolulu rejected Shanti's allegations and found that she had defamed the three Canadians.What is the cult controversy?The three Canadians were not members of Shanti's online community. However, they became targets of her online attacks because of their connections to former followers.Paula Haygarth, one of the people awarded damages, was the stepmother of Amanda Brady, a former Shanti follower from Regina who had been part of her online community for eight years.Brady told CTV News that Shanti had systematically turned her and her daughters against Haygarth."She would message me and say, 'Oh, your energy came into my awareness today. And so I looked at it, and Paula's doing witchcraft on your family. You're in danger. You need to book a session with me,'" Brady recalled.Brady said she spent tens of thousands of dollars on Shanti's sessions and courses, partly because the latter presented herself as a psychic.Former students told CTV's investigative programme W5 that they had approached Shanti for advice on personal matters, including marriages, children and careers.UK-based cult expert Kacey Baker, who has interviewed around 30 people affected by Shanti, said former followers described an environment in which people became dependent on the online spiritual teacher through coercion and control.Baker alleged that personal information shared by students in confidence was sometimes used as material for smear campaigns or intimidation when they decided to leave the community or challenge Shanti.'Canada becoming dangerous'During the Covid pandemic, Shanti reportedly warned her Canadian followers that the country was becoming dangerous and that they should leave to protect their children.Around two dozen Canadians eventually moved to Florida, which Shanti had promoted as a safe haven. Almost all of them later left the community and returned to Canada.Shanti then attacked former followers and their family members online, calling them demonic, Satanic and child abusers, according to the CTV investigation.Brady described the experience of seeing private information about her life made public."I shared my whole life with this woman. Everything. She knows everything and all of it was put out," she said.Haygarth, who said she had endured years of online abuse, described the jury's decision as a relief."It's just so traumatic to be accused for all of those years for something you never did," she said.'We sold our home to bear legal expenses'The financial award could help the three Canadians recover the substantial legal expenses they incurred during the lengthy dispute. However, they have not received any money from the verdict so far, and it remains uncertain how much they will ultimately be able to collect.Haygarth said her legal bills alone exceeded US$600,000. She and her husband Wade were forced to sell their Saskatchewan home and move into a trailer to manage the financial burden of the case.Shanti said she intended to appeal the verdict. She declined multiple requests from W5 for an interview.In an email to the program, she rejected the allegations against her, writing: "I'm actually not a central character in any story, only a fiction that violent abusive men, child molesters, and the women under their control want so desperately to create. … I sued them. I exposed them. They lashed out."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
